blocks.prompt: The Mushroom With Spots
blocks.text: The mushroom in the picture is real. People call it the fly agaric. Say it FLY AG-a-rik. When it is young, it comes up wrapped in a white skin, like an egg. The red cap pushes through and tears the skin. The white bits stay stuck on top. Those are the spots. Rain can wash them off. The fly agaric is pretty, and it is poisonous. Never eat a mushroom you find outside. Under the mushroom, thin white threads spread through the dirt. Those threads eat old leaves and old wood. The mushroom is just the part that pops up.

blocks.prompt: The Part You See Is the Small Part
blocks.text: You know this mushroom. It is red with white spots, and it shows up in storybooks and games. It is real. Its name is the fly agaric, and it grows in forests all over the north, usually near birch and pine trees. Here is the strange part. The mushroom is not the whole living thing. It is more like an apple on a tree. The rest of it is under your shoes. Thin white threads spread through the soil, thinner than a hair, weaving through dead leaves and old wood. Together those threads are called mycelium. Say it my-SEE-lee-um. The mycelium is the fungus. It has been growing down there quietly, sometimes for years. When it has stored enough food and the weather turns wet, it pushes up a mushroom. The mushroom has one job: make spores and let them go. Spores do the work seeds do for a plant, but they are far smaller. One mushroom can drop billions of them. Then the mushroom rots away, and the mycelium keeps going.

the mushroom is only a small part of a much bigger living thing

4.title: The Mushroom Is the Smallest Part
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Mushroom Is the Smallest Part

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fungi are not plants at all

A mushroom is a fruiting body

blocks.prompt: Not a Plant, Not an Animal
blocks.text: For a long time, people filed fungi under plants. They grow out of the ground, they do not move, so plant seemed close enough. It was wrong. A plant makes its own food out of sunlight. A fungus cannot. A fungus has to find food that is already made, which is the same problem you have, and me. Fungi turn out to be closer relatives of animals than of plants. The way a fungus eats is the part worth knowing. You put food inside your body and then digest it. A fungus does the reverse. It grows into its food, floods it with chemicals called enzymes, and lets the food break apart out there in the soil. Then it soaks up the pieces. A fungus digests the world outside itself and drinks the result. What you call a mushroom is only the fruiting body, the part built to make spores. The living network underneath is the mycelium: threads finer than sewing thread, spreading through leaf litter and rotten logs, sometimes for many yards in every direction. Some of that mycelium does something surprising. It wraps around tree roots and makes a trade. The fungus hands over water and minerals it pulled from the soil. The tree hands back sugar it made from sunlight. The fly agaric in the picture lives that way, tied to birch and pine roots. Both sides come out ahead, which is why most plants on Earth have a fungus attached to their roots right now.

notes: Fly agaric: the storybook mushroom, and a real one
Lignin makes wood tough; white rot fungi break it

blocks.prompt: The Quiet Engine Under the Forest
blocks.text: Walk into a forest and you are walking on the roof of something enormous. Every autumn a forest drops an immense weight of leaves, and every year old trees fall. None of it piles up. Something takes it apart and hands the pieces back. That something is mostly fungi. Wood is difficult to eat. It is stiffened with lignin, a tough tangled substance that most living things simply cannot break. A group of fungi called white rot can. They grow their threads into a fallen log and release enzymes that pull the lignin apart, and over years the log softens, darkens, and finally crumbles into soil. The carbon and the minerals locked inside it go back into circulation, ready for the next tree. Without that work, a forest would eventually bury itself in its own dead wood. The threads doing this are called mycelium, and they are the actual organism. A mushroom is only its fruiting body, thrown up for a few days to release spores. That is why mushrooms seem to appear overnight. The fungus is not building them from nothing. The structure is already there underground, folded and waiting, and a good rain lets it pump full of water and inflate, the way a tent goes up in minutes after weeks of packing. The mushroom in the picture is a fly agaric, the red cap with the white flecks that storybooks have used for centuries. The flecks are shreds of a white veil the whole mushroom wore as it emerged. It is beautiful, it is genuinely poisonous, and it is also generous: its mycelium sheathes the roots of birch and pine and trades them water and minerals for sugar. The scale of all this is easy to underestimate. In a forest in eastern Oregon, one honey fungus has been mapped across roughly 2,385 acres, growing outward from a single starting point for something like 2,400 years. It is one continuous organism, and almost nobody standing on top of it would notice a thing.

6.title: The Mushroom Is the Smallest Part
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Mushroom Is the Smallest Part

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Amanita muscaria, the fly agaric
The spots are shreds of a torn universal veil
Hyphae are the threads; mycelium is the network
White rot fungi are among the few things that digest lignin
Mycorrhiza: about 9 in 10 plant species use it
Armillaria ostoyae in Oregon: one organism, 2,385 acres

blocks.prompt: The Fungus Under Your Feet
blocks.text: Almost everyone can draw a mushroom. Red dome, white dots, a pale stalk. That drawing is not invented. It is a fly agaric, Amanita muscaria, a real mushroom of birch and pine forests across the northern world, and it has decorated illustrations for so long that most people assume it is a cartoon. It is not. It is poisonous, it is common, and it is almost entirely misunderstood, starting with the dots. The dots are not markings. A young fly agaric pushes up from the soil sealed inside a white membrane called the universal veil, wrapped like an egg. As the cap swells it splits that membrane, and the torn remains cling to the red surface as flecks. Heavy rain can wash them off, and a spotless fly agaric confuses people who thought the spots were part of the design. They were the packaging. The larger misunderstanding is the mushroom itself. It is not the organism. It is the fruiting body, a temporary structure the organism builds to release spores. The organism is underneath: a network of threads called hyphae, thinner than a human hair, branching endlessly through the soil and known collectively as mycelium. A handful of forest soil can hold miles of it. The mycelium may live for decades or centuries. The mushroom lasts a week. Judging a fungus by its mushroom is like judging an apple tree by one apple, except the tree is invisible and the apple is the only part that ever surfaces. Fungi make a living in a way that has no real parallel among plants or animals. A plant builds its own food from light. An animal swallows food and digests it internally. A fungus does neither and both: it grows directly into whatever it intends to eat, releases enzymes that dismantle the material outside its body, and absorbs the fragments. Digestion first, ingestion second. That reversal is why fungi can eat things nothing else will touch. Wood is stiffened by lignin, a chaotic, irregular polymer that resists almost every enzyme evolution has produced, and a specialized group known as white rot fungi break it down anyway. Because they do, a forest recycles itself instead of drowning in its own timber. Whatever else fungi are, they are the reason dead things go away. Not all of the relationship is destruction. Roughly nine out of ten plant species grow with fungi laced around or into their roots, an arrangement called mycorrhiza. The fungus, whose threads reach where roots cannot, delivers water, phosphorus and nitrogen. The plant, which can do the one thing the fungus cannot, delivers sugar. The fly agaric lives exactly this way, wrapped around birch and pine roots, and the most storybook organism in the forest turns out to be a working partner in the economy that keeps the forest standing. The scale is the part that unsettles people. In Oregon's Malheur National Forest, a single honey fungus, Armillaria ostoyae, has been traced across about 2,385 acres, one genetically continuous individual estimated at 2,400 years old or more. There is no landmark. You could walk across it for an hour and see nothing but trees. This is roughly the point where popular accounts reach for the phrase wood wide web and describe a forest as a wired network trading nutrients and warnings between trees. The underground connections are real and measurable. What the phrase does with them, cooperative forests, mother trees deliberately feeding their young, is a much larger claim, and in 2023 a group of researchers reviewed the field and reported that the evidence from real forests is thinner and more mixed than the popular telling suggests. That is not a scandal. It is what an argument looks like while it is still being had, and it is a useful reminder that the most repeated fact about fungi may be the least settled one. The reliable version is quieter and strange enough on its own. Under the leaves, without light, without a nervous system, without moving, something has been eating the forest and feeding it at the same time for thousands of years, and it announces itself once a season by pushing a red dome into the air.
